steps.message: Reviewing the intake and the question.

claims.text: The goal is to cut grid electricity 30% by 2030 and keep critical loads running in outages, with a capital budget of $750,000 in budget year 2027.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Efficiency only (Scenario A) is estimated to cut 6.2% to 17.6% of annual grid use, so it does not reach the 30% goal. It costs $65,824 to $226,165.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Efficiency plus a budget-capped solar array (Scenario B) is estimated to cut 50.8% to 66.6% of annual grid use and reaches the goal, within budget. It gives no backup power in an outage.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The full path (Scenario C: deeper efficiency, the whole free roof and a backup battery) is estimated to cut 93.1% to 100% of annual grid use and covers about 8 to 9.4 hours of critical loads. It costs $134,342 to $728,885 more than the budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Meeting both the 30% goal and outage backup may take more than $750,000. Whether to extend the budget is the owner's decision once the gap is compared with the estimated savings.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Red Hook Recreation Center (NYC Parks) at 155 Bay Street, Brooklyn is a flat-roofed park recreation center built in 1936 with 27,069 sq ft of floor area and a roof area of 32,860 sq ft, as entered by the user. The utility is Con Edison.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Annual grid electricity of 375,066 kWh (kWh is energy over time) is the working baseline. It matches the city's 2024 building energy report (375,066 kWh). The goal baseline is electricity bought from the grid, which the existing solar already lowers.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Existing solar of 11.4 kW (kW is how much power at one moment) is already on the roof and is taken into account. The city's roof-solar record lists it with estimated output of 12,540 kWh a year.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The plan assumes no other existing efficiency work or renewables, because none were reported. Lighting type, controls and cooling type were not given. Efficiency work already done would lower the savings below.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: The city's building footprints show four buildings on the lot totaling 32,862 sq ft of ground area, close to the 32,860 sq ft roof area entered. A footprint is not a measured roof, and the roof area is the user's number to confirm with an engineer or roofer.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city record flags this lot as a landmark and the building is on NYC Parks land. The building also uses natural gas (about 3,073,752 kBtu, thousand BTU, in 2024), which an electricity goal does not cover.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Solar output is shown as a range from system losses of 18% (low) to 10% (high) around the standard 14% default; weather is typical-year data.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Usable roof area is taken as 55% of the roof, to leave room for setbacks and access.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: About 66 sq ft of usable roof is needed per kW of panels.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Critical load was not given, so it is estimated at 1.0 W per sq ft (27.1 kW, not metered) and backup is assumed at 8 hours. Battery size is 255 kWh after 85% round-trip efficiency.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Efficiency measures (LED and controls) save 10-20% of annual use. This is a planning estimate, not a cited benchmark and not a building model.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Prices are planning-level benchmarks, not quotes, from completed NYC projects (NYSERDA data). Standard efficiency saves 10-20% and deep efficiency 15-25%; these percents are planning estimates, and only 62%-88% of them is counted because the City's audited projects delivered that share.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The baseline is 375,066 kWh a year of grid electricity. A 30% cut is a target of about 112,500 kWh a year.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Standard efficiency (LED lighting and controls) is estimated to save 23,254 to 66,012 kWh a year, which is 6.2% to 17.6% of use. Only 62% to 88% of predicted savings is counted because the City's audited projects delivered that share. The underlying 10-20% saving is a planning estimate.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Efficiency alone is estimated to deliver only 21% to 59% of the 30% goal, so it is a first step and not the whole answer.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Because lighting type, controls and cooling type were not reported, measures already installed cannot be excluded. Already-completed work would lower both the savings and the confidence in them. Confirm these in the audit.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Usable roof is estimated at about 18,073 sq ft, enough for about 273.8 kW DC of panels on the whole roof.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: With 11.4 kW already installed, about 262.4 kW DC of free roof capacity remains. A second whole-roof array is not planned on top of the existing one.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: A 262.4 kW array is estimated to produce 314,134 to 345,150 kWh a year (central 329,667), at a 10-degree tilt facing south.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: At the central output, new solar is about 88% of annual use. At the full range, rooftop solar alone is about 84% to 92% of annual use. On paper this exceeds the 30% goal, but only if the roof can carry the array.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Annual solar bill savings for the full array are estimated at $62,230 (low output, 19.81 cents per kWh) to $83,457 (high output, 24.18 cents per kWh). Prices are the New York commercial average, not this building's own tariff.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The solar output may be partly different if the roof is shaded or if panels must be set back further for the landmark, roof access, or flood and wind design. Roof condition and replacement year are unknown, and the city's roof record gives no roof condition or solar-ready status. None of the cost totals include roof repair or replacement, so a roofer's quote is needed before solar.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenario A (efficiency only): reduction 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use, 21% to 59% of the goal. Does not reach the 30% goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario A: typical upfront cost range $65,824 to $226,165 (median of similar NYC projects about $144,025). Net cost is the same, since no credit applies. Simple payback is 4.1 to 49.1 years; it is not the full SAM model. Within budget. Outage backup: 0 hours.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B (efficiency plus 139.6 kW of solar, capped to the budget): reduction 50.8% to 66.6% of annual use, 169% to 222% of the goal. Reaches the goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B: typical upfront cost range $418,771 to $750,000 (median about $562,870); net cost after the federal credit $312,887 to $592,849 (median about $437,217). Simple payback 5.2 to 15.7 years (not the full SAM model). Within budget at the top of the range. Outage backup: none, because panels shut off in an outage without a battery.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C (deeper efficiency, 262.4 kW whole free roof, 255 kWh battery): reduction 93.1% to 100% of annual use, 310% to 333% of the goal. Reaches the goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C: typical upfront cost range $884,342 to $1,478,885 (median about $1,149,168); net cost after the federal credit $643,568 to $1,121,410 (median about $860,452). Simple payback 7.1 to 16.2 years (not the full SAM model). Over budget: it costs $134,342 to $728,885 more than your budget. Outage backup 8 to 9.4 hours.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: In Scenario C the roof could produce up to about 52,598 kWh a year more than the building still uses. This surplus is potential that flows to the grid and is not counted in savings, because export credits depend on net-metering rules that were not checked.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The budget comparison uses the upfront cost before any federal credit. The model treats $750,000 as one total upfront capital figure, not year by year.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Scenario B, efficiency line: typical range $65,824 to $226,165 (median of similar NYC projects about $144,025), for about 56,260 kWh saved a year at $1.17 to $4.02 per kWh saved, from the middle half of completed NYC public-sector projects (NYSERDA data).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B, rooftop solar line: typical range $352,947 to $523,835 (median about $418,845), for 139.6 kW at $2,528 to $3,752 per kW, from the middle half of 239 completed NYC non-residential projects of 100-500 kW since 2022 (NYSERDA data).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B, federal credit line: about $105,884 to $157,151 off (median about $125,653), counted only because the federal elective pay program is listed as open.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, deeper efficiency line: typical range $81,764 to $287,301 (median about $186,783), for about 75,013 kWh saved a year at $1.09 to $3.83 per kWh saved (NYSERDA data on completed NYC public-sector projects).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, rooftop solar line: typical range $663,347 to $984,525 (median about $787,200), for 262.4 kW at $2,528 to $3,752 per kW (NYSERDA data on completed NYC projects).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, backup battery line: typical range $139,230 to $207,060 (median about $175,185), for 255 kWh at $546 to $812 per kWh, from the middle half of 56 completed or approved NYC storage projects (NYSERDA data). The battery size rests on an estimated load.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, federal credit line: about $240,773 to $357,475 off (median about $288,715), counted only because the program is listed as open.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The federal elective pay (direct pay) credit for governmental entities is listed as open, as of 2026-10-19. Solar must be placed in service by 2027-12-31, and whether NYC Parks qualifies is not confirmed. The credit lowers net cost only; it does not change the upfront budget comparison.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The NYSERDA NY-Sun commercial solar incentive could not be confirmed from an official page, so it is uncertain and left out of every net cost figure. Check the dashboard in a browser.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: NYC's sustainable roofs rule (Local Laws 92 and 94 of 2019) is a rule, not an incentive. It applies to certain major roof renovations, which would require solar, a green roof, or both. It matters if the roof is replaced before solar.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Roof repair or replacement is not in any cost total. The roof's age is unknown, so a roofer's quote is needed.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 0, confirm data and budget: gather 12 months of Con Edison bills and the tariff, confirm the capital budget and its 2027 timing, meter or list the true critical loads and the backup hours wanted, and confirm the roof replacement year.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 1, professional reviews: a licensed structural PE or RA analysis of the roof and a roof condition survey, including the verified usable roof area, before any design is final.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 2, efficiency measures: an energy audit, then LED lighting and building controls if not already installed, and cooling-system upgrades for the gym.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 3, permits and interconnection: Department of Buildings permits through a licensed electrician, FDNY rooftop access review, the Landmarks Preservation Commission advisory report, flood-zone review, and the Con Edison interconnection application.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 4, solar installation: a budget-capped array (about 139.6 kW) fits within $750,000. A larger array up to 262.4 kW is the next step if the budget is extended. Time the work against the 2027-12-31 federal in-service date.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 5, battery, commissioning and verification: a battery sized from the confirmed critical loads, with inverters and switchgear above the design flood elevation, then a check against 12 months of bills. Ask installers to price solar plus battery together and compare the total with the budget.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: The critical loads named are gym cooling, lighting and communications for a cooling center.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Scenario C is estimated to carry the critical loads for about 8 to 9.4 hours in an outage.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenarios A and B give no backup power. Solar panels shut off in an outage without a battery, so the budget-capped plan alone does not meet the outage requirement.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The battery is 255 kWh and 27.1 kW, from an estimated load of 1.0 W per sq ft and an assumed 8 hours. A cooling center may need more load or longer hours in a long outage, so this size is a planning estimate and not metered.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The FEMA map shows flood zone AE at this address, a special flood hazard area, and the building flooded in Hurricane Sandy. Put the battery, inverters and switchgear on the roof or above the design flood elevation.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Only the current FEMA flood zone was read. Heat and winter-storm ratings were not looked up, and the 2015 preliminary flood map was not checked.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: This plan cannot certify that the roof can hold panels. A licensed structural PE or RA must do the structural analysis, together with a roof condition survey.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: A licensed electrician, an FDNY rooftop access review and a Con Edison interconnection review are required before solar or a battery. The list at the end of the plan has the official links.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Flood-zone review under NYC Building Code Appendix G is needed because the address is in zone AE.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: The city record flags the lot as a landmark. Because it is also on parkland, the Landmarks Preservation Commission gives the owning agency an advisory report, not a permit, before rooftop or exterior work. A parkland use review by counsel is also needed.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: The owner is NYC Parks, so approvals go through the agency's capital process. Confirm the route with the agency.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: The roof replacement year was not given. Roof condition and age are not in the city's roof record either. Solar confidence is lower until a roofer and engineer confirm the roof and the usable area.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Confirm first: the city's tax-lot record lists this lot at 140 Lorraine Street with 21,600 sq ft of gross floor area, while the entered address is 155 Bay Street with 27,069 sq ft. The city energy report also shows 27,069 sq ft. The entered values were kept as the working figures.
claims.label: FACT

claims.label: FACT

roadmap.footer_note: All figures are planning estimates with ranges, not quotes. A licensed PE or RA must review the roof structure before design.
roadmap.plain_answer: You asked how to cut grid electricity 30% by 2030 and keep critical loads running in outages on $750,000. On paper the goal can be reached. A roof array sized to fit your budget is estimated to cut grid purchases by about 51% to 67%, at a typical cost of $418,771 to $750,000, but it gives no backup power in an outage. The full path adds deeper efficiency and a battery. It is estimated to cut 93% to 100% and cover about 8 to 9 hours of critical loads, but it costs $134,342 to $728,885 more than your budget. Whether to extend the budget is your decision once you compare that gap with the savings. The figures count electricity bought from the grid, and the 11.4 kW of solar already on the roof is treated as existing. The building sits in a mapped flood zone, is a landmark on parkland, and still needs structural and roof reviews. The battery size rests on an estimated load and an assumed 8 hours. Next, confirm your bills, critical-load figures and budget timing. Then commission the structural and roof reviews and ask for quotes with the battery and electrical gear placed above flood level.
